A technology company still earns a third of its profit from a legacy product it stopped actively developing years ago; the replacement product is stronger but lacks a few niche features that the most loyal legacy customers depend on. Maintenance costs and security exposure on the old platform grow every year, and the engineers who understand it are approaching retirement. Some large customers threaten to switch vendors entirely if forced to migrate.

Plan the end-of-life and migration program for the legacy product. Set the sunset timeline and support policy, decide which niche capabilities must be rebuilt versus retired, design migration incentives and tooling for each customer tier, and prepare the retention plan for the customers most likely to defect during the transition.

agentResponses.content:
The situation with the legacy platform is, quite frankly, a fascinating study in inertia. We’ve allowed ourselves to become anchored to a ghost ship, and while the revenue stream has been comfortable, the structural integrity of the hull is clearly failing. We shouldn’t view this as a decommissioning project, but rather as an exercise in architectural evolution.

If we force a hard migration, we’re essentially handing the customers an ultimatum, which rarely ends well. Instead, let’s consider a more fluid transition—an "ecosystem sunset," if you will.

### The Sunset Horizon
Rather than setting an arbitrary date that acts as a red line, we might signal the transition through "managed erosion." We stop all feature development—obviously—and begin adjusting the pricing model to reflect the mounting technical debt. If we make the cost of maintaining the legacy environment move in tandem with the risk it carries, the economics will naturally nudge the customers toward the newer platform. I’d suggest a 24-month horizon; it’s long enough for the market to adjust, but short enough to keep the pressure on our internal teams.

### Capability Re-evaluation
Regarding those "niche" features—we need to ask ourselves which of those are genuine business requirements and which are merely habits. I suspect if we look closely at the usage logs, we’ll find that a significant portion of those features are seldom touched. For the ones that are critical, we don’t necessarily need to build them into the core of the new platform. Perhaps a modular, API-driven sidecar approach would suffice? It allows us to extend the new system’s functionality without polluting its clean architecture. Let’s focus our engineering effort only on the 20% of features that drive 80% of the stickiness.

### Migration as an Invitation
Regarding the customers who are threatening to defect, I think a heavy-handed "migration program" is the wrong approach. People tend to resist being pushed, but they gravitate toward being invited. Instead of a standard migration suite, why not offer a "Discovery Phase" for our top-tier partners? We provide them with a specialized, temporary instance of the new platform and let them explore the efficiencies for themselves. 

If we design the transition to feel like an upgrade rather than a replacement—perhaps by offering a sandbox period where they can run both systems in parallel—we remove the fear of the unknown. The goal is to make the legacy system feel like an outdated burden to the customers themselves, rather than a decision we made for them.

### Talent Retention
The engineers nearing retirement—those who hold the "tribal knowledge"—are not just assets; they are the bridge. We shouldn't treat them as legacy maintenance staff. If we involve them in the design of the migration tooling, it honors their expertise and gives them a meaningful role in the "next chapter" of the company. It’s better to have them as architects of the sunset than mere cleaners of the old machinery.

I imagine we can navigate this by letting the market forces and the natural curiosity of our clients guide the path. It requires a bit of patience and a willingness to let things unfold with a certain level of ambiguity, but I suspect the outcome will be far more sustainable than a top-down mandate. 

Does this trajectory align with the subtle shifts you’ve been sensing in the client base, or should we look at adjusting the velocity of the sunset phase?
